title: Rogue-tail fair-batcher experiment notes
content:
Status / context:
We observed intermittent p99 spikes on the small-traffic lane (SLA: 150ms p99) for text-generation endpoints using continuous batching. Spikes correlate with small single-request arrivals during peak throughput. The goal of this doc is to capture an exploratory sweep focused on fairness adjustments (urgency weighting, age bias), timeout tuning, and micro-batch formation heuristics to reduce the rogue-tail behaviour without harming throughput or average latency.

High-level hypothesis:
1) Rogue tails are driven by small hot requests being repeatedly preempted by batch coalescing heuristics keyed to throughput optimization (aggressive timeout to form larger batches).
2) Allowing tiny, urgent batches to bypass backpressure (bounded by token budget) will reduce p99 at the cost of a small throughput loss and slightly higher median latency for some cohorts.
3) KV cache interactions and per-core contention (CUDA stream queuing) amplify spikes when mixed small/large batches land on the same worker.

Experiment matrix (runs):
- Variables:
  * max_batch_size: [8, 16, 32, 64]
  * max_wait_ms (timeout): [1, 5, 10, 25]
  * urgency_bias: [0.0 (none), 0.25, 0.5, 1.0]  -- multiplier on age score
  * microbatch_threshold_tokens: [0, 64, 256]  -- tokens considered "tiny"
  * per-worker soft-reservation: [off, 2slots, 4slots]
- Primary metrics to capture (per-run): p50/p90/p95/p99, throughput (tokens/s), batch-size distribution, CPU/GPU utilization, kernel queue depth, KV-cache hit ratio, tail request queuing time.

Testbed / env:
- Model: 7B-refactor-v2 (fp16), sequence len: 1024 average, tail up to 2048
- Nodes: dedicated inference pool (g5.12xlarge style equivalent), 8 workers per pool, 1 GPU per worker
- Clients: synthetic traffic generator that reproduces production arrival patterns (mix of chat short requests ~1-10 tokens vs long generation 200-800 tokens), Poisson arrival with controlled bursts.
- Duration per configuration: 30 minutes steady-state after 10-minute warmup.
- Observability: eBPF traces on scheduler queue, per-request trace ids, per-batch KV cache usage logs, nvprof sampling collected for flagged mid-run anomalies.

Run notes / interesting observations:
- Run A (baseline): max_batch_size=64, timeout=10ms, urgency_bias=0.0, microbatch_threshold=0
  * p99: 370ms (bad), p95: 120ms, median: 28ms, throughput: 82k tokens/s
  * Batch distribution heavily skewed to size 32-64. Small arrivals waited ~12-18ms before flush, often coalesced into big batches -> large variance.
  * NVidia kernel queue showed transient spikes; several tiny requests experienced head-of-line blocking behind large batch kernel launches.

- Run B (small timeout): max_batch_size=64, timeout=1ms, urgency_bias=0.0
  * p99: 215ms (improved), p95: 130ms, median: 34ms, throughput: -6% vs baseline
  * Many more tiny batches formed; higher kernel launch rate increased GPU idle-to-active transitions. Energy but improved tail.

- Run C (urgency bias enabled): max_batch_size=64, timeout=10ms, urgency_bias=0.5, microbatch_threshold=64
  * p99: 180ms, p95: 110ms, median: 30ms, throughput: -3%
  * Urgency weighting bumped small requests ahead in queue formation; batch sizes mixed but tiny requests frequently sent as microbatches. p99 improvement without huge throughput loss.

- Run D (soft reservations): max_batch_size=64, timeout=10ms, urgency_bias=0.5, microbatch_threshold=64, per-worker soft-reservation=2slots
  * p99: 140ms, p95: 115ms, median: 32ms, throughput: -4%
  * Soft reservation prevents all tiny requests stacking on same worker; improved fairness across workers; KV-cache hit ratio slightly down (more misses) causing some tail tokens to fetch slower, but overall latency better for tail.

Profiling deep-dive (what the traces showed):
- eBPF traces show small requests frequently waited at coalescer for timeout window and then were shoved into a large batch. The large batch kernel takes 70-120ms depending on sequence length; tiny request then saw an additional kernel wait -> large end-to-end latency.
- Per-worker NVTX regions: when kernel queue depth > 3, per-request latency variance grows superlinearly. Root cause appears to be serialized kernel launches combined with single-stream device context per worker.
- KV-cache contention: when many tiny microbatches land concurrently on a worker, the KV cache (LRU) shows churn and increased lookups to slower backing store. This aligns with our hypothesis that microbatching can increase cache thrash if not spread.

Tradeoffs / takeaways:
- Aggressively low timeout (1ms) reduces p99 but increases launch rate and can lower throughput modestly (~6-10%). Energy & cost tradeoffs to discuss with infra.
- Urgency bias + per-worker soft reservations yields the best p99 (~140ms) while keeping throughput within a few percent. This is the current recommended direction for prod pilot.
- Microbatching without worker spread worsens KV-cache behavior; mitigation: hash-based routing for tiny requests to spread them evenly or soft reservations.

Actionable next steps (short term):
1) Implement urgency_bias=0.5 default with microbatch_threshold_tokens=64 behind a feature flag. Rollout to 10% of traffic on dedicated pool. (Owner: Riya)
2) Add soft-reservation primitive for workers (2 slots) + routing rule to evenly distribute microbatches (Owner: Ethan).
3) Instrument kernel queue depth metric per worker and add alert when > 3 for >30s (Owner: Lily).
4) Run cost vs energy analysis for lowering timeout to 1ms vs urgency approach (infra/fin).
5) Draft runbook for rollback criteria: if throughput falls >10% or median latency increases by >20% for any high-priority route.

Questions / unknowns to investigate:
- Does urgency_bias interact badly with model-specific runtime variance (decoder-only vs encoder-decoder)? Need per-model sweep.
- How do different quantization kernels affect kernel launch times and thus the benefit of microbatches? Quick test with int8 build pending.
- Is there value in hybrid approach: dynamic timeout that decreases when kernel_queue_depth high? That might reduce unnecessary launches during noisy periods.

Raw datapoints (sample) from key runs (CSV-like):
run,config,max_batch_size,timeout_ms,urgency,micro_thresh,soft_res,p50_ms,p95_ms,p99_ms,throughput_tokens_s
A,base,64,10,0,0,off,28,120,370,82000
B,fast-timeout,64,1,0,0,off,34,130,215,77000
C,urgency,64,10,0.5,64,off,30,110,180,79500
D,urgency+reserve,64,10,0.5,64,2slots,32,115,140,79000

Notes to add to runbook / playbook (practical advice):
- If rolling out urgency_bias, default to conservative value (0.25->0.5). Monitor both p99 and GPU kernel launch/sec counters.
- Combine soft reservations with consistent hashing on request smallness to avoid draining KV cache hotness into one worker.
- Provide a throttled fallback route: if per-worker kernel queue > 6, temporarily increase microbatch threshold to force more coalescing.

TL;DR:
Use urgency bias + per-worker soft reservations as the preferred starting point to reduce rogue tails. Extreme low timeouts help but cost throughput and GPU efficiency. Spread tiny microbatches across workers to avoid KV-cache thrash.

Appendix (commands & links):
- Synthetic traffic harness: repo: github.com/redwood-inference/traffic-sim, config used: experiments/rogue-tail/poisson-mix-2024-10.yaml
- Profiling commands: run nvprof --summary --csv -o /tmp/nvprof-runA.csv on worker capturing suspected interval
- eBPF probe: sudo ./sched-ebpf-trace --pid <scheduler-pid> --dump 30s > /tmp/sched-trace-A.log
- Related PRs: PR#732 (batcher rework), PR#716 (kv-cache telemetry), RFC#485 (fairness scoring)

Unresolved: schedule a whiteboard with infra + kernel team to discuss per-worker multi-stream execution feasibility and potential to batch kernel launches more efficiently (Owner: Marco).

End of notes.
